larder:The Lleó market, for the galley.name: The Lleó market, for the galley
larder:The Lleó market, for the galley.teaser: Be under the Lleó's roof by seven: the day-boat fish and the farm stalls are at their best before ten
larder:The Lleó market, for the galley.story: Treat the Lleó as a dawn errand. Walk in as the shutters lift, while the fish counters still hold the Llançà and Roses day-boat catch. Work outwards: salt cod, a farm's goat cheeses, then the pagès stalls for apples and roots. In late October, look for salsafins and wild mushrooms. The hall and its people have their own card in the tables.
larder:The Lleó market, for the galley.why: Shop the fish first and the cheese last, so nothing warms in the bag.
facts: Day-boat fish at Peixateria Salvador (stalls 74–75, 91–93), salt cod and brandada at Món Salat (78–80), Mas Alba goat cheeses at El Petit Productor (56–59), botifarra dolça, Poma de Girona apples; salsafins from October to April
Monday to Friday 07:00–14:00, Saturday to 14:30, closed Sunday (seen Jun 2026); 07:00–10:00 for the best fish. 29 October is the city's Sant Narcís holiday: check before going

sources.label: Fires de Sant Narcís 2026 programme (29 Oct holiday)

larder:Mercat de la Devesa.name: Mercat de la Devesa
larder:Mercat de la Devesa.teaser: Twice a week a long open-air market of produce, cured meat, dried fruit and cheap shirts sets up by the Ter
larder:Mercat de la Devesa.story: On Tuesday and Saturday mornings vans arrive before nine and a long avenue of awnings goes up: crates of tomatoes and peppers, cured sausages hanging from rails, sacks of almonds and dried apricots, then racks of clothes, kitchen pans and bedding. It is the city's marxants market, licensed by the council, and it moves with the seasons between the shaded avenues of the Devesa park and the banks of the Ter. Expect pagès voices calling prices in Catalan and the smell of roasting chicken at the far end.
larder:Mercat de la Devesa.why: Come for the dried fruit and nuts for the boat's stores; they are cheaper here than in the shops.
facts: 09:00–13:30 under the municipal ordinance (Oct 2026); a 2025 council revision is reorganising the stalls, so check the current pitch
Before 10:00, while the produce stalls are full and the paths are clear
Seasonal vegetables, cured meats, dried fruit and nuts; household goods at the far end

larder:The organic producers' market.name: The organic producers' market
larder:The organic producers' market.teaser: A few farmers carrying the Catalan organic seal, selling their own eggs, vegetables and sheep's dairy
larder:The organic producers' market.story: This is a small gathering rather than a market hall: a handful of growers and herders, each certified by the CCPAE, the Catalan organic council, selling what they produced themselves. The table is short and seasonal, with muddy leeks and chard in October, boxes of eggs, jars of sheep's-milk yogurt, a farm cheese, a bottle of oil. Because the rule is that the seller made it, you can ask how the hens are kept or when the cheese was made and get a first-hand answer.
larder:The organic producers' market.why: Buy the sheep's-milk dairy for the crew breakfast; it rarely reaches the shops.
facts: Thursdays in the old guide; we could not confirm the 2026 day or pitch, so ask at the Mercat del Lleó
Fruit and vegetables, eggs, sheep's-milk dairy, olive oil and cheese, all with the CCPAE organic seal

larder:Fesols de Santa Pau.name: Fesols de Santa Pau
larder:Fesols de Santa Pau.teaser: Small white beans grown in the crater country of the Garrotxa, and sold only in sealed DOP packs
larder:Fesols de Santa Pau.story: Around Santa Pau the fields are dark, crumbly volcanic earth, low in acid, and three old bean varieties grow there: Tavella Brisa, Setsetmanera and Gra Petit. The EU protected them as a DOP in 2015. The beans are small with thin skins, so they cook to a creamy centre without splitting. Only a dozen or so growers remain, and in a lean year the harvest comes to only 20 to 25 tonnes, which is why the packs sell out before the next crop. Sold loose, a bean could be from anywhere; the sealed pack is the guarantee.
larder:Fesols de Santa Pau.why: Eat them once with grilled botifarra in a Garrotxa village, then buy packs for the galley.
facts: Dried beans of three local varieties (Tavella Brisa, Setsetmanera, Gra Petit) from the volcanic soils of Santa Pau and nearby Garrotxa villages; DOP under EU Regulation 2015/1312
Dried and sold all year, cooked or in jars as well as dry; stocks run short before the new crop in poor years
Only in the denomination's own sealed packaging, never loose: Garrotxa grocers and the Girona markets
Botifarra amb fesols, the grilled sausage with the beans dressed in its fat, best in Garrotxa village kitchens

larder:Poma de Girona.name: Poma de Girona
larder:Poma de Girona.teaser: Firm, sharp apples from the orchards between Girona and the Empordà, under an EU seal since 2003
larder:Poma de Girona.story: Drive out of Girona towards the sea in September and the plain is ruled into orchards, nets over the rows, bins stacked at the field edges. The picking lasts about three months, yet the fruit is eaten all year from cold store. The IGP, registered in 2003, covers a small set of familiar varieties grown here; warm days and cool nights in the Ter valley give them a firmer bite and more acid than the same apples from elsewhere. A recent harvest came to around 89,000 tonnes.
larder:Poma de Girona.why: Buy a bag of Granny Smith for the galley; they hold up in a tart and in a long week aboard.
facts: IGP apples (EC Regulation 1491/2003) from the Girona plain; Golden, Gala, Granny Smith and Red Delicious carry the seal
Picked from late summer into autumn, sold from cold store all year; new-crop apples are in the markets now (Oct 2026)
The farm stalls of the Mercat del Lleó and any Girona greengrocer; look for the IGP label
Raw and cold, or fried in slices beside botifarra

sources.label: Eurofresh Distribution — PGI Poma de Girona

larder:Formatge Garrotxa.name: Formatge Garrotxa
larder:Formatge Garrotxa.teaser: A goat's cheese with a grey-blue velvet rind, named for a comarca where almost nobody makes it
larder:Formatge Garrotxa.story: Cut a Garrotxa and you find a pale, close paste under a soft grey-blue mould, smelling of cellar and hazelnut. It is made only from whole goat's milk and comes in rounds of about one kilo or half a kilo. The style took the Garrotxa's name, but when the EU registered it as an IGP in December 2023 the zone was drawn around all of Catalonia, and Catalan public broadcaster 3Cat counted twelve makers, only one of them inside the comarca. So the name is a style, not a postcode.
larder:Formatge Garrotxa.why: Ask the cheesemonger which farm made it; the makers differ more than the label suggests.
facts: Goat's-milk cheese with a grey-blue bloomy rind, 1 kg or 0.5 kg; IGP since December 2023 (Reg. 2023/2872), with a production zone covering all of Catalonia
Cal Formatger in the Barri Vell and the cheese stalls of the Mercat del Lleó
On a board with a glass of Empordà white, at room temperature
Ripening time: the old guide gave at least 21 days, other descriptions say four to six weeks; we did not find the minimum in the official specification

larder:The Empordà estates.name: The Empordà estates
larder:The Empordà estates.teaser: Low bush vines bent by the tramuntana, and family cellars an hour north that pour for visitors who book
larder:The Empordà estates.story: North of Girona the Empordà plain rises towards the Albera and the Rodes hills, and the vines there are short, gnarled bushes kept low against the north wind. The appellation dates from 1975 and covers roughly 1,700 hectares. Most of its cellars are family affairs that open by appointment: you drive up a farm track, a son or daughter of the house walks you through the rows, and the tasting happens at a kitchen table or in a new winery beside the old mas. The grapes have their own cards under Drink.
larder:The Empordà estates.why: Book one long visit with a vineyard walk rather than three quick tastings.
facts: Espelt (Vilajuïga), La Vinyeta (Mollet de Peralada), Masia Serra (Cantallops), Terra Remota (Sant Climent Sescebes), all in the Alt Empordà
Mostly by appointment; Espelt runs a visit of about 2.5 hours in Catalan, Spanish, English or French (Oct 2026)
Garnatxa and Carinyena reds, whites of Garnatxa blanca and roja, the sweet Garnatxa de l'Empordà, at the cellar door
Espelt's visit with tasting €27 on the DO Empordà listing (Oct 2026); others vary
Through each cellar, found in the DO Empordà winery register; Espelt on +34 671 546 206

sources.label: Consell Regulador DO Empordà — Espelt Viticultors

larder:Oli de l'Empordà.name: Oli de l'Empordà
larder:Oli de l'Empordà.teaser: A grassy, faintly bitter oil from the Argudell olive, pressed on the plain each November
larder:Oli de l'Empordà.story: The olive groves of the Empordà are scattered between vineyards and wheat, many of them old trees of Argudell, a variety you rarely meet outside this corner of Catalonia. A bottle of the DOP must hold at least half Argudell, with Curivell, Llei de Cadaqués and Arbequina making up the rest. The new oil arrives in November, cloudy and peppery, catching the back of the throat. Drizzled on bread rubbed with tomato, or over a suquet just before serving, it tastes of cut grass and green almond.
larder:Oli de l'Empordà.why: Buy this year's oil in November, when it is greenest, and keep it out of the sun aboard.
facts: DOP olive oil (EU Regulation 2015/385) from the Alt and Baix Empordà and parts of the Pla de l'Estany and Gironès; at least 51% Argudell
Pressed from November; sold all year
Producers include Empordàlia (Oli de Pau) and Olis Bàrbara; about €12–25 a bottle (seen Jun 2026)
On pa amb tomàquet, or raw over fish stew

larder:Cal Formatger's board.name: Cal Formatger's board
larder:Cal Formatger's board.teaser: Taste the province on a board first, then have the same farmhouse cheeses wrapped to take back to the boat
larder:Cal Formatger's board.story: Use the board as a tasting before you buy. Order it cut from the Girona comarques, note which rounds the table keeps reaching for, then have those wrapped for the galley. Ask for a Cerdanya washed rind, a Garrotxa raw-milk blue and a soft spoon cheese, and say how long you will be at sea. The shop's own card is in the tables.
larder:Cal Formatger's board.why: Tell them the passage length; they will pick younger or riper cheeses to match.
facts: The cut-to-order board, then whole cheeses to take: Puigpedrós (Molí de Ger), Glauc (Formatgeria Xauxa, Les Preses), Garrotxa goat's cheeses
Opens 10:30, closed Sunday and Monday, and shuts mid-afternoon most days (seen Jun 2026)
Walk in to buy; ask ahead for a private tasting
Boards from €25 to €55 in four sizes (seen Jun 2026)

walks:Passeig de la Muralla.name: Passeig de la Muralla
walks:Passeig de la Muralla.teaser: Walk the top of the old city wall, tower to tower, with the cathedral on one side and the plain on the other
walks:Passeig de la Muralla.story: The rampart path runs along walls first raised in the 9th and 10th centuries, when Girona was a Carolingian frontier town facing al-Andalus, laid on Roman lines from the 1st century BCE. You climb a stair and the city drops away: terracotta roofs, washing lines, the cathedral's grey bulk close enough to count its buttresses. Every so often a tower lets you climb higher, and from the top the view runs across the Ter plain to the hills. The path dips and climbs on narrow steps, and costs nothing.
walks:Passeig de la Muralla.why: Climb every tower you pass; each frames the cathedral from a new angle.
facts: Jardins dels Alemanys, behind the cathedral
Narrow paved path with steep stairs; not suitable for wheelchairs or pushchairs
Late afternoon, when the light warms the stone
The tower tops for the cathedral and the Barri Vell roofs
Water in summer; the path has little shade. Entry is free

sources.label: AAA TripCanvas — Passeig de la Muralla

walks:Cathedral to Sant Feliu.name: Cathedral to Sant Feliu
walks:Cathedral to Sant Feliu.teaser: From the top of the cathedral's ninety steps down to Sant Feliu, before the city wakes
walks:Cathedral to Sant Feliu.story: Go at eight, when a street sweeper and the pigeons have the Plaça de la Catedral to themselves. Stand at the head of the Baroque staircase, ninety steps of grey stone, and look down over the old town before you descend. A few minutes downhill the lanes open onto Sant Feliu, the city's older great church, where Roman and early-Christian tombs are built into the walls of the apse. It is a short walk, but almost every stone on it is older than the street plan around you.
walks:Cathedral to Sant Feliu.why: Do it before breakfast, when the steps are empty and the bells carry.
facts: The top of the cathedral staircase, Plaça de la Catedral
About 30 minutes, longer if you go inside
Stone stairs and steep cobbled lanes
The view from the head of the staircase, then the sarcophagi at Sant Feliu; both churches have their own cards under Culture
Shoes with grip for the worn steps

walks:The Call, lane by lane.name: The Call, lane by lane
walks:The Call, lane by lane.teaser: Narrow stepped alleys of dark stone, where the medieval Jewish quarter folds back on itself
walks:The Call, lane by lane.story: Turn off Carrer de la Força and the street narrows into stairs, passages and dead ends between tall houses of dark stone. This was the Call, Girona's medieval Jewish quarter and one of the best preserved in Europe; in the 13th century the scholar Nachmanides taught Kabbalah here. Light reaches the bottom of the lanes only around midday, and voices echo off the walls. Lose the map for twenty minutes, then finish at the Centre Bonastruc ça Porta, whose museum has its own card under Culture.
walks:The Call, lane by lane.why: Go mid-morning before the tour groups, and let yourself take the wrong turning.
facts: Steep steps and polished stone that turns slippery in rain
The Museu d'Història dels Jueus at the Centre Bonastruc ça Porta, to end the walk
walks:The Call, lane by lane.maps_query: Carrer de la Força, Girona, Spain

walks:The Onyar bridges.name: The Onyar bridges
walks:The Onyar bridges.teaser: Cross the Onyar bridge by bridge, with the ochre and rust river houses doubled in the water below
walks:The Onyar bridges.story: The houses along the Onyar stand straight out of the river in a row of ochre, rust, pink and cream, a palette fixed during a 1980s restoration led by the painter Enric Ansesa with a team of architects. Zig-zag across the footbridges and watch them shift. Stop on the Pont de les Peixateries Velles, the red riveted-iron bridge put up in 1877 by Gustave Eiffel's company; whether Eiffel drew it himself is disputed, but the firm and the year are documented. From its middle the cathedral rises behind the façades.
walks:The Onyar bridges.why: Stand mid-span on the iron bridge at golden hour, when the reflection is sharpest.
facts: Pont de les Peixateries Velles, on the Mercadal bank
Golden hour, or early morning when the river is still
The cathedral rising behind the river houses from the iron bridge
Eiffel's own hand in the bridge's design; the company and the date, 1877, are not in doubt
walks:The Onyar bridges.maps_query: Pont de les Peixateries Velles, Girona, Spain

walks:Parc de la Devesa.name: Parc de la Devesa
walks:Parc de la Devesa.teaser: Forty hectares of gravel avenues under thousands of plane trees, mostly planted in 1850
walks:Parc de la Devesa.story: Cross to the Mercadal side and the light turns green. About 2,600 plane trees stand in strict rows here, most of them planted around 1850, their trunks mottled grey and cream and their crowns more than fifty metres up. The avenues are gravel, and the only sounds are footsteps, bicycles and old men playing petanca. On a hot afternoon it is several degrees cooler than the streets. In late October the park becomes the fairground for the Fires de Sant Narcís, 23 October to 1 November in 2026, which have their own calendar card.
walks:Parc de la Devesa.why: Sit on a bench in the middle avenue at four on a hot day and do nothing.
facts: Passeig de la Devesa, by the Mercadal
About 40 hectares of park; a loop of the avenues is short and flat
Hot afternoons; in late October expect the fair
The view straight down the central avenue of planes

walks:Vall de Sant Daniel.name: Vall de Sant Daniel
walks:Vall de Sant Daniel.teaser: Ten minutes past the walls, a wooded valley of springs leads to a Romanesque monastery
walks:Vall de Sant Daniel.story: Leave the old town by Sant Pere de Galligants and follow the stream inland. Within minutes the houses thin, the lane narrows between kitchen gardens and plane trees, and you hear water: the valley is fed by springs, and at the Font del Ferro an iron-rich trickle stains its basin orange. Behind Montjuïc the city disappears entirely. The walk ends at the monastery of Sant Daniel, a Romanesque church in a walled garden. In August this is the coolest walk in Girona.
walks:Vall de Sant Daniel.why: Taste the iron water at the Font del Ferro, then sit by the monastery wall.
facts: Plaça de Sant Pere de Galligants
Quiet paved lane, then earth tracks; gentle climb
The Font del Ferro and the monastery of Sant Daniel
walks:Vall de Sant Daniel.maps_query: Sant Pere de Galligants, Girona, Spain

walks:Castell de Sant Miquel.name: Castell de Sant Miquel
walks:Castell de Sant Miquel.teaser: Climb through holm oak to a ruined castle at 385 m, with the four-river plain spread below
walks:Castell de Sant Miquel.story: From Sant Pere de Galligants the path follows the Vall de Sant Daniel past the monastery, then turns uphill into holm oak, the city noise fading behind you. After about an hour and a half you come out at the broken walls of the Castell de Sant Miquel on its summit. The view repays the climb: the plain where Girona's four rivers meet, the Pyrenees to the north, and on a clear morning a pale line of the Costa Brava to the east, which has its own guide.
walks:Castell de Sant Miquel.why: Leave early, before the haze builds, to see the Pyrenees from the top.
facts: Plaça de Sant Pere de Galligants
About 9.6 km there and back, with about 330 m of climbing
About 1 h 25 up and 1 h 10 down
Signed paths and forest tracks; medium difficulty
The summit view from the ruins, 385 m up
Water and sturdy shoes; there is no café on the way
